"MR. DELTA OF PSI UPSILON"
ORRIN S. WIGHTMAN, DELTA '95
Frank E. Booth, Delta 11, made the
following remarks at the 1961 Founders'
Day Dinner in New York City, in pre
senting a citation to Brother Orrin S.
Wightman, Delta '95:
"We have met here tonight to venerate
the Founders of our
Fraternity. They built
on the solid rocks of idealism, group
solidarity and brotherly affection. Chang
ing times have not tarnished their luster.
The great leaders of our
Fraternity have
fostered the same
spirit. Brother Orrin
Sage Wightman, Delta 1895, has illumi
nated the ideals of our Founders.
"Brother Wightman was born in New
York City on
May 6, 1873, the son of
Frederick Butler Wightman, Delta 1851,
and Abigail Ann Hartley. He was
gradu
ated from New York University in 1895
and in 1898 received his M.D. from New
York University. After interning at Gouverneur
Hospital and City Hospital, he
went into practice in 1900.
"He became consultant at
City Hos
pital, Midtown, Nyack, Bayonne, St.
John's Riverside and Yonkers General. He
was
especially identified with the Poly
clinic, where he served as Professor of
Internal Medicine.
"Brother Wightman has been President
of the State Medical Society�being now
the oldest surviving President�the County
Medical Society and Editor in Chief of the
State Medical Journal. He became a Fel
low of the Academy of Medicine in 1905
and has been for many years a member of
the Council and Board of Trustees of the
Academy and is at present Chairman.
Three years ago, the Academy gave
Brother Wightman a Testimonial Dinner
which filled every available seat in the
ballroom of the Waldorf Astoria.
"During World War I, Brother Wightman was a member of the mission to Rus
sia, with the rank of Major. His book, 'An
American Physician in the Russian Revolu
tion' has been a valuable contribution to
the literature of that period.
"Brother Wightman has been for many
years President of the Hudson River Coun
try Club. His other clubs are the Univer
sity, Lotos, Metropolitan, Explorers, Wianno and American Yacht.
"In photography�which is his chief
hobby�he was for some
years President of
the Oval Table Society and is an
Honorary
Member of the Photographic Society of
America and a Fellow of the Royal Pho
tographic Society of Great Britain. Of spe
cial note is the book he produced, by way
of pictures, entitled "Early Days of Coastal
Georgia."
"As Trustee of the Dula Foundation,
Brother Wightman has made innumerable
contributions to charities of various kinds�
this has been of special interest to the
Delta.
"His brother, Percy B. Wightman, was
Delta '93; his brother, Robert S. Wightman, was Delta '97, and his father was
Delta, 1851. His uncle, Isaac Hartley, was
also a Delta man.
"His cousin, M. Hartley Dodge, is a
member of the Lambda Chapter, class of
1903, where his support has meant much to
Columbia University .
"The greatness of Brother Wightman
lies in his stewardship�of his fortune, of
his time and of his ideas. It has been of
inestimable value to the Psi Upsilon Fra
ternity.
"When the smoke of battle cleared away
at the close of World War II, he discov
ered that the Delta Chapter was
being
kept alive by a few loyal graduate broth
ers. Tom Rickenback was the pnly under
graduate at one time and Eugene Foley at
another. Brother Wightman thought: "My
help is needed. This is the Fraternity of
my Father, my Brothers and my Uncle."
He replaced many things which were
broken and missing when the army re
turned our House. He gave thoughtfully.
For example, he told the first new mem
bers, 'I will furnish paint and brushes if
you will do the work.'
He then created the Orrin Sage Wightman Endowment Fund for the Delta. One
of his greatest gifts has been the gift of
himself. He has been present at every
meeting of the Delta Corporation for many
years. His ideas and personal presence

"Quiet Voice with a Big Stick. . , ."
Brigadier General Frank L. Howley,
Delta '25, was the principal speaker at
New York's Founders' Day Dinner. Fol
lowing are his remarks:
"In thinking in terms of the Soviet Un
ion and the communist
conspiracy there is
always a
big element of bluff in die Soviet
actions. It should not, however, be as
sumed that because the Soviets are
bluffing
that they will not carry out their threats.
Rather, it should be said that the Soviets
play their cards to the maximum and take
chances. However, they are in the position
of a
poker player who has some good cards
in his hand and knows exactly what the
other players have in theirs.
"The Soviet system of espionage in the
world is something which has never before
been known to mankind. The traders who
went ahead of the armies of Genghis
Khan to scout out the enemy positions
were children in the operation in compari
son to the espionage system employed by
the Soviet Union.
"The second thing to bear in mind, in
judging the Soviets, is that they are never
confined, in their demands and their
threats, to one
spot in the world. Berlin
is the focal point at the moment. They
want us to look at Berlin, to worry about
Berlin, and to give up our honor in Ber
lin but, at the same time, they are con
tinuing their underground and overground
operations to get control of Laos, South
Vietnam, Algeria, the Congo RepubUc,
Portuguese Angola and trade unions in New
York City.
"This all-out war which is being waged
against us
by the Soviet Union should be
no
mystery to us. It has been outlined
again and again by their proclamations
starting with those of Karl Marx, as inter
preted by Lenin, later by Stalin and now
by Khrushchev.
"The Soviet bluff in Berlin is really not
a bluff in the normal sense of the word. It
was
approached very cautiously. Before
the Soviets took their bold action in Berlin
and delivered ultimatums, they were sure
that they would succeed. In the case of
the wall which they had built across the
city, they had actually accomplished the
separation of the Eastern part of Berlin
from the Western parts of Berlin way back
at the end of the Soviet-imposed blockade
of the city which ended on
May 12, 1949.
"At that time, after the Western powers
and the West Berliners had been intimi
dated and threatened during the blockade
of Berlin, representatives of the United
States. Britain and France humbly went to
Paris and negotiated with the Soviets who

had perpetrated the crime. A crime which
cost us 72 lives in the Airlift, cost us over a
bilHon dollars, and made us suffer an in
sult such as America had not before experi
enced from any nation.
"At Paris, a status
quo was
agreed to
that in effect permitted the Soviets to get
away with their crime. It permitted them
furthermore, and more to the point, to
continue to control completely and uni
laterally one third of the city of Berlin. It
was this concession which permitted them
to take out of Allied control the Eastern
part of Berlin which paved the way for
the operations now
against all of Berlin.
Likewise, since the Second World War,
the Soviets have been able, contrary to
AUied agreements, to maintain complete
control of one third of Germany. They have
set up a
stooge government there and have
assured the world many times that it is a
sovereign government. The more recent
threats to sign a
peace treaty are, on the
face, silly and should have been labelled
as nonsense. At least six times, to
my mem
ory, the Soviets have announced that their
stooge government in East Germany and
East Berlin is an
independent sovereign
government. Khrushchev's signing of
another peace paper should be labelled as
simply the signing of another piece of pa
per. Instead of that, we have taken his
threats, ultimatums and bluffs too seri
ously and have built the situation up into
a
major conffict. East vs. West. Many
times, in deahng with the Soviets, it is
better to take off a shoe and hammer the
table, in answer to a Soviet shoe hammer
ing, than it is to take too seriously the vul
garity of leaders who are
basically vulgar.
"I feel reasonably sure that Khrushchev
himself was
surprised at the reaction to his
statement that he was
going to sign a
peace treaty with East Germany. On an
American radio program at that time I
treated it very fightly, stressing only one
point: Regardless of what the stooge gov
ernment of East Germany talked about and
regardless of Khrushchev's talk, neither he
nor the East Germans had better, in any
way, interfere with the entrance or exits
of the Western Powers, and the people un
der their control, to or from West Berlin.
If our word had any weight in interna
tional councils, a
simple statement along
those lines would be enough. Unfortu
nately, as President Kennedy has said, our
military forces in Berlin are
hostages. The
rest of the sentence, however, which I ut
tered some five years ago, was that our
troops were there as
military hostages be
cause the world didn't believe in the words
of our
diplomats. We simply have to stop
making strong speeches and then not
matching our
strong words with strong
actions. The quiet voice with the big stick
is stiff good foreign policy.
"Most of the world is confused by the
inconsistencies of American foreign policy
during the past years. This is not an indict
ment of either party alone. It is an indict
ment of our
policies which too frequently
reflected the indifference and contradic
tions of the American people themselves.
"Unless we
simplify our
thinking to the
fundamental principles and stop playing to
the grandstands to please people who
couldn't care less about the United States,
we are in for worse trouble than we are in
now. However, if our
government will re
flect the simplicity, the vigor, the honor
and the courage of the American people
we can move forward with confidence in
our domestic as well as
foreign affairs."

WORLD RENOWNED LIBRARIAN
HARRY CLEMONS, XI "02
Harry Clemons, Xi '02, who retired as li
brarian of the University of Virginia on
June
30, has served in that post since 1927. The
collections of cataloged printed books have
grown during his administration from 150,000
to more than 575,000 volumes, the manu
scripts from a few thousand to over 3,500,000
pieces, while picture and print collections of
50,000 and map collections of 68,000 items
have been assembled. The general library had
seven full-time staff members in 1927 and
63 in 1950.
Brother Clemons was
graduated from Wes
leyan University in 1902 with the B.A. degree,
receiving the M.A. at the same university in
1905, and the Litt.D. in 1942. Pursuing post
graduate studies as a Scribner Fellow at
Princeton University, 1903-04 (M.A. 1905),
and a
Jacobus Fellow of Princeton at Oxford
University, 1906-07, he later studied in the
School of Library Service at Columbia Uni
versity in 1927. Beginning as a
library assist
ant at Wesleyan in 1902, he served as in
structor of English at Princeton, 1904-06 and
1907-08, and reference librarian of Princeton,
1908-13. A year after his appointment as
pro
fessor of English (1913-1920) in die Univer
sity of Nanking, China, he became librarian
of the same university, a
position which he
held�with a brief "furlough" interlude in
1922 with the Chinese Collection at the Li
brary of Congress�until the Communist up
rising (the "Nanking Incident") of 1927, when
he returned to the United States and began
the librarianship at Virginia.
Some of the milestones in his library ad
ministration included, at Princeton, the expan
sion of library service coincident with the
establishment of the preceptoral system by
President Woodrow Wilson; at Nanking, the
organization of a
college library, the develop
ment of its services in ways appropriate to
Chinese needs, and the training of a Chinese
staff; and at Charlottesville, only a few items
will be mentioned from a list that might be
greatly expanded. Such are the recataloging
of the printed books in the Library of Con
gress classification; the appointment in 1930
of the university's first archivist as a
library
official, and the campaign and planning for
the Alderman Library; the compilation, 19331943, of the checklist of the surviving papers
of Thomas Jefferson; the acquisition by the
university of such special collections as the
McGregor Library of Americana and English
Harry Clemons, Xi '02
literature, the Lomb optical collection, the
Mackay-Smith music collection, the Stone li
brary on the history of printing, the Streeter
collection on southeastern railways, the Sadleir-Black coUection of Gothic novels, die Tay
lor collection of American novels, and the
Victorius collection on evolution; and the
activities of the University of Virginia library
as publisher of the Annual Report on Histori
cal Collections (20 reports to date), of the
University of Virginia Bibliographical Series
(nine volumes to date), and of the publications
of the McGregor Library (of which eight have
already been issued). Brother Clemons would
himself earnestly disclaim any part in many
of these and other projects except approval.
To quote his own words, he insists that he has
merely "helped to create and maintain an
atmosphere in which new ideas would have
free motion" and that he has had "an amaz
ingly alert and original group of associates."
Over all the 23 years of his librarianship
at Virginia, Brother Clemons has striven un
tiringly for the development of the library as
a research institution and as an institution
for willing service; for the raising of the pro
fessional standards of his own staff and of hbrarians throughout Virginia; and above all
for the fostering of the cooperative spirit

When receiving the Thomas Jefferson
Award, he was
given the following citation:
"Harry Clemons, who has served this Uni
versity since 1927, is not only a
great li
brarian in a
generation of able librarians. He
is in many respects unique. In an
age of
specialization he has retained universal in
terests. In an
age of science he has found in
the humanities a
great deal more than a
refuge. Beginning his work in a
day when
scholarship was assumed in a librarian, he
has survived with distinction the generation
that has demanded of librarianship the tech
niques of corporate management.
"The creative work of Harry Clemons in
this academic community has been char
acterized by our own
James Southall Wilson
as 'the best job' done at the University in his
time. That work has been anonymously as
sociated with much tliat the University of
the first half of this century will be remem
bered for. Jefferson's biographer, Dumas Ma
lone, hailed our tenth librarian as 'the living
embodiment of the Jeffersonian tradition,' who
in Jefferson's own
country 'brought that tradi
tion to life in the twentieth century and gave
it an institutional scope which not even the
far-seeing Founder could have anticipated.'
"In the present company of scholars the
bestowal upon Harry Clemons of the Thomas
Jefferson Award will come as a
surprise to
no one but its modest recipient."

NEW YORK UNIVERSITY SITE
OF 1962 CONVENTION
THE
Delta Chapter wiU be host to the
fraternity on the occasion of the 120th
Convention of Psi Upsilon on
1962. This will be the Delta's 4th Conven
tion marked by the celebration of the 125th
anniversary of the founding of the "Branch
of Psi Upsilon."
Headquarters for the convention will be
on the University Heights campus of New
York University at 183rd St. in the Bronx.
New York University is the world's larg
est privately controlled university.
New York University was
granted its
charter by the state of New York on
April
18, 1831. The intention of its founders was
to establish a
university "on a liberal foun
dation, which shall correspond with the
spirit and wants of our
age and country,
which shall be commensurate with our
great and growing population, and which
shall enlarge the opportunities of educa
tion for such of our
youth as shall be found
quahfied and inclined to improve them."
Owing to the limitations of the original
public subscription, the first instruction
was restricted to the traditional classical
studies then current in American colleges
and universities. In 1835, however, the
Council approved a
plan for legal instruc
tion drawn up by Benjamin F. Butler, At
torney General in Jackson's and Van Buren's cabinets, thus inaugurating the first
of its professional divisions. And in the au
tumn of that year the University moved
into its first permanent quarters, a Gothic
structure begun in 1833. Next in order of
establishment was the Medical Depart
ment, later the College of Medicine, in
which instruction was
begun in 1841. The
College of Medicine (renamed School of
Medicine in 1960) has expanded into the
comprehensive New York University Medi
cal Center.
The University Bulletin issued in the
spring of 1854 announced the establish
ment of a "School of Civil Engineering
and Architecture." In 1899 the program
was
enlarged to include degrees in civil,
chemical, and mechanical engineering; In
1920 the present designation. College of
Engineering, was
adopted.
With the organization in 1886 of the
Graduate School of Arts and Science the
University entered a
period of expansion in
graduate and professional study commensu
rate with the vision of its founders; the first
of its kind to be established on the univer
sity plane of professional schools of law,
medicine, and theology.
The School of Commerce, Accounts, and
Finance, not only one of the largest schools
of the University but also the largest of its
kind in the country, was
organized in 1900.
From it, in turn, was
developed the Gradu
ate School of Business Administration.
In 1894 the undergraduate hberal arts
and engineering programs were removed to
the new
campus at University Heights.
The College of Dentistry was estabhshed
in 1925 when the New York College of
Dentistry, an
independent school founded
in 1866, was
incorporated into the general
University structure. The Graduate School
of Public Administration and the Graduate
School of Social Work complete the list of
